questions.question: A stable adult has a new focal seizure and progressive unilateral weakness. CT suggests an intra-axial mass. Which next diagnostic approach is most appropriate?
options: Contrast-enhanced structural brain MRI with specialist tissue-diagnosis planning
Lumbar puncture for cytology before further structural imaging
MR spectroscopy as a substitute for tissue diagnosis
Interval noncontrast CT after an antiseizure-treatment trial
questions.explanation:
Investigation of a Suspected Intracranial Tumor

Correct answer: Contrast-enhanced structural brain MRI with specialist tissue-diagnosis planning

Define the Lesion and Its Immediate Consequences

**Standard structural MRI is the initial detailed investigation for suspected glioma when feasible.** NICE specifies T2, FLAIR, diffusion and pre- and post-contrast volumetric T1 sequences.

Assess location, enhancement, diffusion, edema, hydrocephalus and mass effect. Imaging guides the differential, operative planning and the safest tissue approach.

CT remains useful for rapid emergency assessment and selected questions such as hemorrhage or calcification, but is not interchangeable with the complete MRI evaluation.

Imaging Does Not Replace Integrated Diagnosis

**Coordinate specialist neurosurgical and neuro-oncology assessment.** Glioma, metastasis, lymphoma, infection and inflammatory lesions can share imaging features.

Advanced perfusion or spectroscopy can help selected uncertainties but should not be presented as histologic or molecular confirmation.

Avoid LP when mass effect or a dangerous intracranial pressure gradient makes it unsafe; removing only a small volume does not remove that risk. Treat seizures and other urgent complications while planning diagnosis. If rapid deterioration occurs, stabilization and urgent structural intervention take priority over an elective sequence; in this stable patient, high-quality imaging supports an informed tissue and treatment decision.

Lumbar puncture for cytology before further structural imaging: CSF cytology has selected oncologic roles, but an incompletely assessed mass can create unsafe pressure gradients; define the structural lesion and procedural safety first.

MR spectroscopy as a substitute for tissue diagnosis: Spectroscopy can refine selected imaging questions, but metabolic patterns are not sufficiently definitive to replace integrated tissue diagnosis when feasible and clinically appropriate.

Interval noncontrast CT after an antiseizure-treatment trial: Seizure treatment is needed, but symptomatic control does not establish the mass etiology or justify delaying definitive structural assessment in progressive focal disease.

questions.question: An adult diffuse glioma has oligodendroglial morphology and an IDH mutation. Which additional finding is required for the integrated diagnosis of oligodendroglioma?
options: Homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion
MGMT promoter methylation
An isolated TERT promoter mutation
Whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion
questions.explanation:
Integrated Diagnosis of Oligodendroglioma

Correct answer: Whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion

Use Molecular Identity Rather Than Morphology Alone

**Oligodendroglioma is defined by an IDH mutation and whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion.** A fried-egg appearance or calcification can suggest the diagnosis but cannot establish it.

Partial chromosomal losses are not equivalent to the defining whole-arm event. An apparently discordant assay result requires neuropathology review and an appropriate confirmatory strategy.

ATRX loss and TP53 abnormalities favor an astrocytic pathway in an IDH-mutant diffuse glioma and influence the testing algorithm.

Separate Identity, Grade and Treatment Prediction

**Adult-type diffuse gliomas comprise IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant/1p19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma and IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.** Each combines molecular identity with relevant grading features.

Oligodendrogliomas have CNS WHO grades 2 or 3. An IDH-mutant astrocytoma can be grade 2, 3 or 4; grade alone does not convert one lineage into another.

MGMT methylation and other biomarkers answer different clinical questions. Treatment depends on integrated diagnosis, grade, symptoms, resection and patient factors rather than one microscopic descriptor. Ensure the final report supports multidisciplinary planning, and do not apply a glioblastoma regimen automatically to every infiltrating glioma with an aggressive-looking scan.

Adult diffuse entity | Defining molecular framework | CNS WHO grades

Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant | IDH mutation; astrocytic integrated lineage | 2, 3 or 4

Oligodendroglioma | IDH mutation plus whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion | 2 or 3

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype | Appropriate adult diffuse astrocytic context, IDH/H3-wildtype and qualifying histologic or molecular features | 4

Homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion: CDKN2A/B deletion has important grading implications in IDH-mutant astrocytoma, but is not the defining additional marker of oligodendroglioma.

MGMT promoter methylation: MGMT methylation informs alkylator sensitivity in relevant contexts, but does not define the oligodendroglial lineage or substitute for 1p/19q codeletion.

An isolated TERT promoter mutation: TERT mutations are common in oligodendroglioma but also occur in other tumors; they are not sufficient to establish the integrated diagnosis.

questions.explanation:
Molecular Grade 4 IDH-Mutant Astrocytoma

Correct answer: Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, CNS WHO grade 4

A Molecular Alteration Can Determine Grade

**Homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion is a grade-4 marker in IDH-mutant astrocytoma.** Necrosis or microvascular proliferation can also establish grade 4, but are not required when this defining alteration is present.

Distinguish homozygous deletion from a nonspecific copy-number change or a report that does not establish the relevant alteration. Review technical adequacy and integrated pathology.

This rule should not be transferred uncritically to every tumor class; molecular grading is entity-specific.

Preserve the Integrated Name

**The correct name remains astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 4**, rather than the older IDH-mutant glioblastoma terminology.

The distinction matters for prognosis, counseling and clinical-trial interpretation. Similar grade numbers across molecular entities do not imply identical biology or outcomes.

Review surgical sampling, molecular findings and clinical factors in treatment planning. Lack of enhancement or a limited biopsy without necrosis should not falsely reassure clinicians when the validated molecular result changes grade. Conversely, do not infer deletion from a suspicious scan; treatment decisions require the actual pathology evidence and the patient’s condition and preferences.

Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, CNS WHO grade 2: A low-grade histologic appearance does not override the grade-4 implication of validated homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion in an IDH-mutant astrocytoma.

Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, CNS WHO grade 3: Grade 3 can apply to other IDH-mutant astrocytomas, but this molecular alteration supports grade 4 even without the sampled histologic grade-4 features.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4: The patient’s tumor is IDH-mutant; assigning grade 4 does not change the molecular identity into IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.

questions.explanation:
Molecularly Defined IDH-Wildtype Glioblastoma

Correct answer: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4

Molecular Findings Can Establish Grade-4 Biology

**Adult IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic gliomas can meet glioblastoma criteria through molecular features**, even without sampled necrosis or microvascular proliferation.

Relevant features include EGFR amplification, combined whole-chromosome 7 gain and chromosome 10 loss, or a qualifying TERT promoter mutation in the appropriate diagnostic context.

Confirm the molecular result and exclude alternative entities, particularly in younger patients or unusual locations. IDH-wildtype alone does not make every CNS tumor a glioblastoma.

Do Not Confuse a Screening Stain With Complete Molecular Assessment

**Negative IDH1 R132H immunostaining does not exclude every IDH mutation in all settings.** Additional sequencing is selected according to age, histology and the diagnostic algorithm.

Midline or unusual tumors can need H3 and other molecular assessment. DNA methylation profiling can help resolve selected difficult classifications.

Integrate pathology with imaging and clinical information before treatment planning. A small biopsy can underestimate histologic aggressiveness, while molecular findings can clarify it. Conversely, do not apply a molecular rule outside its intended tumor context or use an isolated nonspecific marker to overrule a well-supported alternative entity. The final integrated name should communicate both identity and grade to the treating team.

Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, CNS WHO grade 4: That diagnosis requires an IDH mutation; a high-grade molecular feature does not make an IDH-wildtype tumor IDH-mutant.

Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted: Oligodendroglioma requires the defining IDH mutation and whole-arm codeletion; EGFR amplification does not substitute for either requirement.

Histologic grade 2 astrocytoma without molecular upgrading: The absence of sampled histologic grade-4 features does not override a qualifying molecular glioblastoma feature in the appropriate adult diffuse astrocytic context.

questions.explanation:
MGMT Promoter Methylation and Alkylator Benefit

Correct answer: MGMT promoter methylation

A Predictive Marker Rather Than a Lineage Definition

**MGMT repairs alkylator-induced DNA damage.** Promoter methylation is associated with reduced expression and greater expected benefit from alkylating treatment in relevant glioblastoma settings.

It does not define oligodendroglioma, establish IDH status or replace the integrated diagnosis. A methylated tumor remains the same molecular entity.

The test is especially useful in older or frail patients when a single-modality strategy is being considered. Performance status, goals, comorbidity and treatment tolerance remain essential.

Apply the Result Without Overstating Certainty

**Methylated tumors are more likely to benefit from temozolomide**, while hypofractionated radiotherapy is often favored over temozolomide alone in an unmethylated patient unsuitable for combined treatment.

Assays and cutoffs vary, and borderline results need careful laboratory interpretation. Methylation is not a guarantee of response or a complete individual prognosis.

Fit adults can receive combined therapy even when the expected chemotherapy benefit is smaller; do not turn a selection aid for a frail single-modality scenario into a universal rule to omit treatment. Discuss myelosuppression, infection, nausea and monitoring as part of the plan, alongside supportive and palliative care aligned with the patient’s priorities.

Whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion: This defines oligodendroglioma in an IDH-mutant context; it is not the main predictive biomarker for alkylator benefit in established IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.

ATRX loss: ATRX is useful for lineage assessment in appropriate diffuse gliomas, but does not replace MGMT methylation when evaluating temozolomide sensitivity in this scenario.

An isolated TERT promoter mutation: TERT can contribute to integrated tumor classification, but is not the principal marker used for this temozolomide-selection question.

questions.explanation:
Maximal Safe Resection Preserves Function

Correct answer: Aim for maximal safe resection using appropriate functional planning and preserve neurologic function

**Maximal safe resection is an individualized functional goal.** Diffuse infiltration limits the meaning of a radiographic complete resection and surgery is not inherently curative.

Use appropriate mapping, monitoring, tract-oriented planning or awake techniques where suitable and available. Their role is to support a safe strategy, not to guarantee absence of deficits.

If safe resection is not feasible, targeted biopsy can provide the diagnosis needed for subsequent treatment. Patient goals and expected morbidity influence the choice.

**Obtain adequate tissue for integrated histologic and molecular assessment.** Sampling quality matters when the lesion is heterogeneous or a small biopsy could miss important features.

Discuss radiotherapy, systemic options and supportive needs after the integrated result. Preserved cognition, communication and mobility can be crucial to completing further therapy. questions.explanation:
Concomitant and Adjuvant Temozolomide

Correct answer: Focal radiotherapy with concomitant temozolomide followed by adjuvant temozolomide

Use the Established Combined Schedule

**The conventional framework combines focal radiation and temozolomide.** The landmark trial used ==60 Gy in 30 fractions== with ==75 mg/m² temozolomide daily== during radiation.

After a treatment break, adjuvant temozolomide is commonly given at ==150–200 mg/m² daily for five days in each 28-day cycle==, for six cycles in the original regimen.

Adapt treatment for performance status, age, marrow and organ function and patient goals. This question does not imply that every older or frail patient should receive a six-week combined course.

Monitor Toxicity and Interpret Response Carefully

**Check blood counts and relevant organ function** and provide antiemetic and infection-prevention measures according to the regimen and steroid exposure.

Lymphopenia and opportunistic infection risk are important during combined treatment. New enhancing abnormalities can reflect treatment effect as well as progression and need clinical-imaging correlation.

MGMT methylation informs expected alkylator benefit but does not guarantee response. Discuss supportive, rehabilitative and palliative care alongside tumor-directed treatment. Do not promise that extending adjuvant chemotherapy indefinitely improves survival; duration and later interventions should follow evidence and the individual clinical course rather than assuming more cycles are necessarily better.

questions.question: An adult has a surgically sampled grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma, with residual nonenhancing disease and no prior radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Immediate chemoradiation is not otherwise required. Which targeted option has trial evidence supporting delayed progression and next intervention in a selected population?
options: Vorasidenib
Osimertinib
Bevacizumab
Dabrafenib with trametinib
questions.explanation:
Vorasidenib in Selected IDH-Mutant Grade 2 Glioma

Correct answer: Vorasidenib

Keep Trial Selection Separate From Broad Glioma Labels

**Vorasidenib inhibits mutant IDH1 and IDH2.** INDIGO studied a selected postoperative grade 2 population with no previous anticancer therapy beyond surgery and without an immediate need for chemoradiation.

It improved progression-free survival and delayed the next intervention compared with placebo. These endpoints should not be restated as proven overall-survival benefit.

The US FDA approved it in 2024 for patients aged 12 years or older with susceptible IDH1/2-mutant grade 2 astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma after surgery. Regulatory availability and local eligibility can differ.

Prescribe With Hepatic and Reproductive Safety Monitoring

**The adult dose is ==40 mg orally once daily== under the prescribing information.** Confirm the susceptible mutation and review drug interactions, smoking effects and reproductive precautions.

Check liver tests before treatment, ==every two weeks for the first two months==, then ==monthly for the first two years==, with additional assessment when abnormalities occur.

Hepatotoxicity can require interruption, reduction or discontinuation under label guidance. Do not substitute this strategy for indicated urgent treatment of enhancing, symptomatic or higher-grade disease outside the supported context. Continue MRI and clinical follow-up and use shared decisions about the benefit of delaying other treatment against toxicity and monitoring burden.

Osimertinib: Osimertinib has CNS activity in selected EGFR-mutant lung cancers, but is not the IDH-targeted option supported for this postoperative grade 2 glioma population.

Bevacizumab: Bevacizumab can reduce edema and has selected recurrent-tumor roles, but does not provide the IDH-directed trial evidence or indication described here.

Dabrafenib with trametinib: BRAF/MEK inhibition can be relevant to selected BRAF-altered tumors, but an IDH mutation does not establish that target or the treatment indication in this question.

questions.question: A small radiologically typical meningioma is found incidentally. The patient has no attributable symptoms, no important mass effect and no documented growth. Which initial approach is most appropriate?
options: Offer upfront stereotactic radiosurgery to avoid future surgical risk
Offer elective resection now based on the imaging diagnosis
Clinical and MRI surveillance with individualized review of growth and risk
Follow symptoms without scheduled MRI surveillance
questions.explanation:
Observation of an Incidental Meningioma

Correct answer: Clinical and MRI surveillance with individualized review of growth and risk

Separate Incidental Disease From a Treatment Indication

**Observation is a first option for an incidental asymptomatic suspected meningioma.** Consider size, location, edema, growth risk, age, comorbidity and the patient’s priorities.

Cognition and subtle focal symptoms should be assessed rather than assuming that no dramatic deficit means no attributable impact.

A radiologic diagnosis is not a tissue grade. Rapid growth or atypical features should prompt reassessment for a higher-grade lesion or another diagnosis.

Intervene When the Balance Changes

**Symptoms, meaningful growth or threatened function can justify intervention.** Surgery provides tissue and decompression; radiosurgery or fractionated radiation can suit selected anatomy and clinical circumstances.

Aim to preserve function, particularly near venous sinuses, cranial nerves or other critical structures. An intentional subtotal approach plus selected radiation may be preferable to a disabling attempt at complete removal.

Define MRI and clinical follow-up with the specialist service and modify it as evidence accumulates. Seizures, visual change or new focal findings warrant reassessment rather than waiting for the next routine scan. Treatment choice should balance disease control against neurological risk rather than treating every imaging discovery or every small size change as an automatic operation.

Offer upfront stereotactic radiosurgery to avoid future surgical risk: Radiosurgery can suit selected anatomy and indications, but immediate treatment is not routinely preferable to surveillance for an incidental low-risk lesion.

Offer elective resection now based on the imaging diagnosis: Resection can be appropriate for symptoms, growth or threatened function, but a small asymptomatic lesion without those features can initially be observed.

Follow symptoms without scheduled MRI surveillance: Symptoms are important, but a planned observation strategy generally includes imaging to assess growth rather than waiting for a clinical deficit.

questions.question: A patient has a large vestibular schwannoma causing brainstem compression and progressive gait impairment. Which treatment principle is most appropriate?
options: Use single-fraction radiosurgery as the initial treatment
Use MRI surveillance with vestibular rehabilitation as the initial strategy
Surgical decompression assessment, with extent and adjunctive treatment individualized to cranial-nerve preservation
Use fractionated radiation before considering surgical decompression
questions.explanation:
Large Vestibular Schwannoma With Brainstem Compression

Correct answer: Surgical decompression assessment, with extent and adjunctive treatment individualized to cranial-nerve preservation

Size and Function Change the Management Pathway

**Vestibular schwannoma management considers tumor size, growth, hearing, cranial-nerve function and mass effect.** Observation, radiosurgery and surgery each have appropriate settings.

Small asymptomatic tumors can be observed with imaging and functional assessment. Symptomatic smaller lesions require individualized comparison of growth control, hearing and facial-nerve risks.

Large tumors compressing the brainstem generally require surgical assessment for decompression rather than applying the small-tumor observation pathway.

Protect Cranial-Nerve and Brainstem Function

**Plan the surgical extent around safe decompression and function.** Selected subtotal or near-total approaches with subsequent observation or radiation can balance control against morbidity.

Discuss realistic hearing and facial-nerve outcomes rather than promising preservation from one technique. Evaluate hydrocephalus, swallowing and other cranial-nerve effects when indicated.

Continue postoperative imaging and hearing or balance rehabilitation. Young age, bilateral tumors or other syndromic features should raise the possibility of NF2-related schwannomatosis and prompt appropriate counseling. Treatment is not chosen from diameter alone, but progressive compression is a distinct indication that cannot be managed solely with symptomatic vestibular medicines.

Use single-fraction radiosurgery as the initial treatment: Radiosurgery is useful in selected smaller tumors, but a large compressive lesion may require immediate mechanical decompression and a different risk balance.

Use MRI surveillance with vestibular rehabilitation as the initial strategy: Observation and rehabilitation can suit selected small or stable lesions, but progressive gait impairment with brainstem compression needs decompression assessment.

Use fractionated radiation before considering surgical decompression: Fractionation can be selected when surgery is unsuitable, but does not make prior neurosurgical assessment unnecessary in a fit patient with progressive compression.

questions.question: A fit patient has biopsy-confirmed primary CNS diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and adequate renal function. Which induction principle is most appropriate?
options: Use focal temozolomide chemoradiation as for newly diagnosed glioblastoma
Use R-CHOP alone as for a typical systemic nodal DLBCL
Use a specialist high-dose-methotrexate-based CNS-active regimen with planned consolidation
Use whole-brain radiotherapy alone as the routine preferred induction for a fit patient
questions.explanation:
High-Dose Methotrexate in Primary CNS Lymphoma

Correct answer: Use a specialist high-dose-methotrexate-based CNS-active regimen with planned consolidation

Achieve Therapeutic CNS Exposure

**High-dose methotrexate is a central component of PCNSL induction.** EHA-ESMO recommends doses of at least 3 g/m² with an appropriate rapid infusion to achieve sufficient CNS exposure.

Combination choices depend on age, performance status and organ function. MATRix is one option for eligible fit patients and combines methotrexate, cytarabine, rituximab and thiotepa.

Do not apply intensive regimens indiscriminately to frail patients. Rituximab use and the balance of efficacy and toxicity require specialist discussion in this setting.

Plan Rescue, Clearance and Consolidation

**Methotrexate requires protocolized hydration, urinary alkalinization, folinic-acid rescue and drug-level monitoring.** Review renal function and interacting medicines before each course.

Delayed clearance or kidney injury needs urgent specialist management; a standard dose cannot be administered safely without the supporting monitoring system.

Responding eligible patients may receive thiotepa-based autologous transplantation or another tailored consolidation strategy. Radiation-related neurotoxicity matters, especially in older adults. Monitor cognitive, ocular and other involved functions and distinguish relapse from treatment toxicity. PCNSL treatment is not simply systemic lymphoma chemotherapy delivered unchanged to a patient with a brain lesion.

Use focal temozolomide chemoradiation as for newly diagnosed glioblastoma: That regimen addresses a different tumor biology; PCNSL requires a lymphoma-specific CNS-active induction and consolidation strategy.

Use R-CHOP alone as for a typical systemic nodal DLBCL: R-CHOP is effective in many systemic DLBCL settings but is not adequate stand-alone induction for PCNSL because CNS drug exposure and disease management differ.

Use whole-brain radiotherapy alone as the routine preferred induction for a fit patient: Radiation can have selected roles, including consolidation or palliation, but fit patients generally receive methotrexate-based induction rather than routine radiation-only treatment.

questions.question: A patient with metastatic solid cancer has a large brain lesion causing progressive weakness and substantial mass effect. A CNS-active systemic drug is available. Which immediate treatment principle is best supported?
options: Proceed directly to single-fraction SRS without neurosurgical review
Start the CNS-active systemic agent and schedule MRI reassessment first
Begin dexamethasone and defer the local decision until steroid taper
Arrange urgent local-treatment assessment and appropriate edema support
questions.explanation:
Symptomatic Brain Metastasis With Mass Effect

Correct answer: Arrange urgent local-treatment assessment and appropriate edema support

Symptoms Change the Sequencing

**Symptomatic brain metastases should receive appropriate local therapy regardless of systemic treatment availability.** Neurosurgical and radiation assessment should address mass effect, anatomy and overall prognosis.

Surgery can relieve compression and provide tissue, particularly when diagnosis is uncertain or a large dominant lesion is driving disability.

Steroids may provide temporary edema relief while definitive planning proceeds, but do not replace tumor-directed local treatment.

Integrate Local and Systemic Options

**Choose the local approach through multidisciplinary review.** Consider lesion number, total volume, location, extracranial disease control, functional status and patient goals.

A large lesion is not automatically suitable for a single radiosurgery fraction; fractionated stereotactic approaches can be considered when surgery is unsuitable, according to anatomy and specialist planning.

Postoperative radiation is often required for durable local control. Continue appropriate systemic therapy through a coordinated schedule rather than treating local and systemic care as mutually exclusive choices. Discuss supportive and palliative options when the expected burden of intervention exceeds benefit; the existence of multiple metastases alone does not eliminate the need to assess a threatening dominant lesion.

Proceed directly to single-fraction SRS without neurosurgical review: SRS can provide local control in suitable lesions, but size and compression can favor surgery or fractionation and warrant multidisciplinary review.

Start the CNS-active systemic agent and schedule MRI reassessment first: A systemic-first approach can suit selected asymptomatic lesions, but symptomatic mass effect generally requires prompt local-treatment assessment.

Begin dexamethasone and defer the local decision until steroid taper: Steroids bridge edema-related symptoms but do not replace definitive assessment of a large compressive lesion or justify waiting through a taper.

questions.question: A patient with good performance status has three small unresected brain metastases, no significant mass effect and a non-small-cell solid-tumor primary. No indication for tissue acquisition is present. Which radiation approach is generally appropriate?
options: Conventional whole-brain radiotherapy as the initial radiation course
Stereotactic radiosurgery to the lesions with MRI surveillance

questions.explanation:
SRS for Limited Small Brain Metastases

Correct answer: Stereotactic radiosurgery to the lesions with MRI surveillance

Select SRS From More Than Lesion Count

**SRS alone is a standard option for suitable patients with one to four unresected metastases**, excluding the small-cell setting addressed differently in the guideline evidence.

Size, total tumor volume, location, symptoms and safe dose constraints matter. Trial populations generally involved relatively small lesions; do not extrapolate the count rule to any tumor volume.

Surgery remains useful for a large symptomatic lesion or when diagnosis is needed, even in a patient who will also receive radiosurgery to other sites.

Surveillance Is Part of the Strategy

**Local control of treated lesions does not prevent every new intracranial metastasis.** Arrange regular MRI and clinical follow-up with access to salvage treatment.

Discuss radionecrosis, edema and delayed imaging uncertainty, along with the cognitive trade-offs of WBRT. Subsequent lesions may require additional SRS, surgery or a broader radiation strategy.

Coordinate systemic cancer care and patient goals. SRS selection does not mean extracranial prognosis is irrelevant or that local therapy should continue irrespective of declining function. Reassess the whole clinical situation at each treatment decision rather than following a fixed lesion-number algorithm without regard to burden and benefit.

Conventional whole-brain radiotherapy as the initial radiation course: WBRT remains appropriate in selected diffuse or otherwise unsuitable disease, but suitable limited small lesions can receive SRS with less broad cognitive exposure.

Resection of the largest lesion followed by radiation to the remaining sites: Surgery helps when tissue or decompression is needed, but neither indication is present here and a suitable SRS strategy avoids an unnecessary operation.

Systemic therapy alone with MRI follow-up irrespective of tumor target: Selected CNS-active regimens permit deferral, but this requires tumor-specific evidence and a defined plan rather than the lesion count alone.

questions.question: A patient appropriately selected for WBRT has no hippocampal lesions and an expected survival exceeding four months. Which strategy best reduces the treatment-related cognitive burden?
options: Hippocampal-avoidance WBRT without memantine
Conventional WBRT with memantine, without hippocampal avoidance
Hippocampal-avoidance WBRT with memantine when technically appropriate
Conventional WBRT with cognitive rehabilitation after treatment
questions.explanation:
Cognitive Protection During Whole-Brain Radiotherapy

Correct answer: Hippocampal-avoidance WBRT with memantine when technically appropriate

Select Eligible Patients

**ASCO-SNO-ASTRO recommends memantine and hippocampal avoidance for eligible WBRT recipients** without hippocampal lesions and with expected survival of at least four months.

The radiation team must confirm that target coverage and avoidance constraints are appropriate. Do not infer eligibility solely from the total number of metastases.

These measures mitigate cognitive injury rather than guarantee that memory will remain normal. Tumor, medicines, seizures and other illness can also affect cognition.

Maintain the Distinction Between Local Therapy Choices

**First decide whether WBRT is the appropriate strategy.** SRS, surgery, systemic approaches or supportive care may be more suitable in other clinical contexts.

When WBRT is chosen, avoid omitting cognitive protection merely because the patient has metastatic cancer. Conversely, an expected very short survival changes the likely benefit and treatment burden.

Assess baseline cognition, renal function and medicine tolerance when planning memantine and follow the applicable prescribing protocol. Continue MRI and clinical reassessment and provide practical cognitive support. A new cognitive decline after treatment should not automatically be labeled radiation toxicity without evaluating progression, metabolic illness and other reversible contributors.

Memantine Trial Regimen

**RTOG 0614 began treatment within three days of starting WBRT**, with escalation to ==20 mg/day== and continuation for ==24 weeks==.

Use a gradual titration and adjust for renal function and tolerability under the applicable prescribing protocol. This is cognitive protection, not tumor therapy.

Hippocampal-avoidance WBRT without memantine: Avoidance helps reduce cognitive burden, but the guideline recommends combining it with memantine in eligible WBRT recipients rather than omitting the medication component.

Conventional WBRT with memantine, without hippocampal avoidance: Memantine provides cognitive protection, but an eligible patient can gain the additional benefit of hippocampal avoidance when coverage constraints permit it.

Conventional WBRT with cognitive rehabilitation after treatment: Rehabilitation can help residual deficits, but does not replace available preventive measures when the patient is eligible for them.

questions.explanation:
Selected Asymptomatic Metastases and CNS-Active Therapy

Correct answer: A multidisciplinary team may select initial CNS-active systemic therapy with a defined surveillance and salvage plan

Deferral Is a Selected Strategy

**Certain CNS-active systemic regimens permit consideration of deferred local therapy in asymptomatic disease.** Molecular subtype and direct evidence for the agent matter.

questions.question: A patient with a brain metastasis has headache and mild focal weakness attributable to edema, without impending herniation. Which initial steroid principle is most appropriate?
options: Use physiologic hydrocortisone replacement and reassess symptoms
Start dexamethasone 16 mg/day and maintain it through all cancer treatment
Start dexamethasone 4–8 mg/day and reassess for taper
Use a brief fixed dexamethasone course and stop without symptom review
questions.explanation:
Dexamethasone for Symptomatic Vasogenic Edema

Correct answer: Start dexamethasone 4–8 mg/day and reassess for taper

Match Dose to the Clinical Threat

**Dexamethasone provides temporary relief of edema-related neurologic symptoms.** A starting total of ==4–8 mg/day== is commonly appropriate for mild or moderate symptoms.

Marked symptoms, elevated pressure or threatening mass effect may require a higher dose, such as ==16 mg/day==, alongside urgent definitive assessment.

The steroid response does not establish the tumor diagnosis or replace surgery, radiation or systemic cancer treatment. Asymptomatic patients do not automatically need prolonged prophylactic steroids.

Reduce Exposure as the Clinical Situation Allows

**Use the lowest effective dose and taper as rapidly as clinically tolerated.** Account for recurrent edema and adrenal suppression after prolonged exposure.

Monitor glucose, infection, mood, sleep, myopathy and gastrointestinal risk. Proximal weakness from steroids can itself reduce mobility and obscure the neurologic assessment.

Coordinate tapering with the treating team and the expected effect of local therapy. Prolonged combined immunosuppression can require infection prevention, including PJP prophylaxis according to risk. Do not abruptly stop a long course or continue it indefinitely because symptoms once improved; both decisions require a current clinical assessment and a documented plan.

Use physiologic hydrocortisone replacement and reassess symptoms: Replacement is appropriate for adrenal insufficiency but is not the recommended anti-edema regimen for this metastatic presentation.

Start dexamethasone 16 mg/day and maintain it through all cancer treatment: Higher doses can suit severe pressure-related symptoms, but mild deficits without impending herniation support lower exposure and active reassessment.

Use a brief fixed dexamethasone course and stop without symptom review: A short course can be appropriate, but taper and cessation should account for clinical response, definitive treatment and prior exposure rather than a fixed unreviewed schedule.

questions.question: A patient with newly diagnosed brain metastases has never had a seizure and is not undergoing an immediate operation. Which antiseizure approach is most appropriate?
options: Start levetiracetam in all patients because it has few enzyme interactions
Do not prescribe routine antiseizure prophylaxis solely because metastases are present
Start valproate to prevent seizures and improve tumor survival
Start phenytoin until the first surveillance MRI documents response
questions.explanation:
Seizure Treatment Differs From Routine Prophylaxis

Correct answer: Do not prescribe routine antiseizure prophylaxis solely because metastases are present

Separate Two Different Clinical Questions

**Routine prophylaxis is not recommended for seizure-naive patients with newly diagnosed brain tumors.** This differs from treating a patient who has already had a tumor-associated seizure.

A first attributable seizure commonly warrants ongoing antiseizure treatment because a structural epileptogenic lesion is present; select the drug from the patient’s broader clinical context.

The perioperative question has a separate evidence base. SNO/EANO found insufficient evidence to recommend routine perioperative medication to reduce seizures, rather than proving that every individual perioperative course is wrong.

Choose Treatment for an Actual Indication

**When medication is needed, review cancer-drug interactions, renal or hepatic function, mood and blood counts.** Non-enzyme-inducing agents are often favored for interaction reasons.

Levetiracetam can affect mood or behavior; valproate can cause thrombocytopenia and hepatic toxicity. Drug tolerability matters in a patient already receiving systemic treatment.

Educate about recognizing seizures and appropriate emergency responses. New episodic symptoms require evaluation rather than retrospective justification of universal prophylaxis. Do not interpret the absence of prophylactic treatment as absence of seizure risk; it reflects the lack of sufficient preventive benefit to outweigh treatment burden in this population.

Start levetiracetam in all patients because it has few enzyme interactions: Levetiracetam is often useful when seizure treatment is indicated, but a favorable interaction profile does not establish benefit from routine prophylaxis in seizure-naive patients.

Start valproate to prevent seizures and improve tumor survival: Valproate can treat selected seizure disorders, but routine prophylaxis and an assumed antitumor survival benefit are not supported reasons to prescribe it here.

Start phenytoin until the first surveillance MRI documents response: Phenytoin can treat seizures in appropriate settings, but preventive use until imaging response lacks a supported indication and adds interactions and adverse effects.

questions.question: Months after stereotactic radiation, a treated metastasis enlarges with surrounding edema. The patient is stable. Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate before assigning tumor progression?
options: Integrate treatment timing, serial MRI and selected advanced imaging, with tissue assessment when needed
Classify progression from enlargement on one conventional contrast MRI
Classify radiation necrosis from improvement after dexamethasone
Use a single perfusion value as definitive proof of pure radiation injury
questions.explanation:
Radiation Necrosis Versus Tumor Progression

Correct answer: Integrate treatment timing, serial MRI and selected advanced imaging, with tissue assessment when needed

Recognize a Post-Treatment Differential

**New enhancement after radiation is not automatically viable tumor.** Timing, prior dose distribution, clinical course and serial evolution help distinguish progression from injury.

The 2026 EANO consensus supports advanced MRI, particularly perfusion, and amino-acid PET in selected difficult cases. No imaging method perfectly excludes mixed tumor and necrosis.

Review the actual treatment plan and images with neuroradiology and radiation oncology. A label based only on a report phrase can lead to an inappropriate change of cancer therapy.

Use the Result to Guide Treatment

**Symptomatic radiation injury may require corticosteroids**, with bevacizumab or surgery considered in selected steroid-dependent, refractory or diagnostically uncertain cases.

Surgery can provide tissue and decompression when feasible, but procedural risk and goals matter. An asymptomatic stable patient can sometimes undergo planned imaging reassessment rather than immediate intervention.

Review bevacizumab-related bleeding, thrombosis and wound-healing concerns before use. Improvement in edema is not proof that all viable tumor is absent. Continue monitoring symptoms, steroid exposure and imaging, and reconsider the diagnosis if the course diverges from the expected response rather than repeatedly treating an unverified mechanism.

Classify progression from enlargement on one conventional contrast MRI: Growth and enhancement can reflect recurrent tumor, treatment effect or both; one conventional scan is not always sufficient to establish mechanism.

Classify radiation necrosis from improvement after dexamethasone: Steroids can reduce edema around viable tumor as well as radiation injury; a response does not uniquely establish necrosis.

Use a single perfusion value as definitive proof of pure radiation injury: Perfusion can help estimate the likelihood of recurrence, but overlap, technical variation and mixed pathology prevent a universal single-value diagnosis.

questions.question: During an ifosfamide-containing regimen, a patient develops acute confusion and somnolence without a new focal deficit. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Interrupt ifosfamide and urgently assess treatment toxicity and competing metabolic, infectious or neurologic causes
Continue the infusion and reassess after the planned chemotherapy cycle
Treat empirically for CNS tumor progression without reviewing the regimen
Give methylene blue as diagnostic confirmation and omit further workup if alertness improves
questions.explanation:
Ifosfamide-Associated Encephalopathy

Correct answer: Interrupt ifosfamide and urgently assess treatment toxicity and competing metabolic, infectious or neurologic causes

Recognize a Potentially Reversible Treatment Complication

**Ifosfamide can cause encephalopathy during or after administration.** Features range from altered attention and behavior to severe reduced consciousness or seizures.

Stop the suspected exposure and assess airway, glucose, electrolytes, renal function, infection and relevant co-medications. Select imaging or EEG according to the examination and course.

Renal dysfunction and other treatment factors can influence risk and clearance. No single bedside feature proves that the drug is the only cause.

Provide Support and Review Rescue Options

**Use supportive care and specialist oncology/toxicology input.** Prescribing information allows consideration of methylene blue, but evidence is limited and it is not a substitute for stopping exposure and assessing physiology.

Review contraindications and interactions, including serotonergic drugs and G6PD-related concerns, before any methylene-blue prescription. Apply the relevant institutional regimen rather than treating it as harmless empirical therapy.

Monitor for recovery and seizures, and reconsider alternative explanations if the course is atypical. Decisions about future ifosfamide exposure require risk-benefit review and a prevention plan; recovery from one episode does not guarantee safe rechallenge. Keep other regimen-specific protective measures coordinated with the oncology team rather than stopping every supportive drug indiscriminately.

Continue the infusion and reassess after the planned chemotherapy cycle: Acute CNS toxicity can be severe; continuing the suspected drug without immediate assessment may increase harm and delays evaluation of competing emergencies.

Treat empirically for CNS tumor progression without reviewing the regimen: Progression can enter the differential, but the temporal drug association warrants toxicity assessment rather than automatic attribution to cancer growth.

Give methylene blue as diagnostic confirmation and omit further workup if alertness improves: Methylene blue may be considered for selected cases, but response is not a specific diagnostic test and does not remove the need to assess other causes.

questions.question: A patient with headache is found to have bilateral optic-disc swelling. Which initial assessment best establishes urgency and helps confirm papilledema?
options: Obtain OCT and use nerve-fiber thickness as the main measure of current visual function
Document acuity and headache severity and use those to determine follow-up urgency
Expert disc assessment, BP measurement and documented visual acuity, pupils and formal visual fields
Arrange LP manometry before ophthalmic characterization of the disc swelling
questions.explanation:
Papilledema Assessment Must Include Visual Function

Correct answer: Expert disc assessment, BP measurement and documented visual acuity, pupils and formal visual fields

Confirm What the Disc Finding Represents

**Papilledema is optic-disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure.** Other disc disorders and pseudopapilledema can look similar and may require experienced ophthalmic review.

Measure BP to identify a hypertensive emergency and examine acuity, pupils, fields and the fundus. Document severity with photographs or OCT when available.

Central acuity can be normal early. Formal fields can reveal important loss that changes urgency even when the patient reports only headache.

Investigate the Cause While Protecting Vision

**Arrange urgent brain imaging with venous assessment when raised pressure is suspected.** Exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and cerebral venous thrombosis before assigning an idiopathic label.

After appropriate imaging and exclusion of contraindications, LP measures opening pressure and checks CSF contents. The safest sequence depends on the clinical condition.

Rapid visual deterioration requires urgent specialist treatment planning rather than routine headache follow-up. Continue objective visual monitoring throughout investigation; reducing headache does not establish that the optic nerves are safe. If disc swelling is uncertain, seek expert confirmation rather than either exposing the patient to unnecessary invasive tests or dismissing possible sight-threatening disease.

Obtain OCT and use nerve-fiber thickness as the main measure of current visual function: OCT helps document swelling and later atrophy, but is not a substitute for visual-field testing or a complete ophthalmic assessment.

Document acuity and headache severity and use those to determine follow-up urgency: Acuity and pain matter, but visual-field loss can precede central acuity loss; formal fields and expert disc assessment are needed to judge visual threat.

Arrange LP manometry before ophthalmic characterization of the disc swelling: LP can be appropriate after imaging and safety assessment, but does not replace confirming papilledema and documenting the visual baseline.

Papilledema Assessment Must Include Visual Function

Correct answer: C — Expert disc assessment, BP measurement and documented visual acuity, pupils and formal visual fields

Confirm What the Disc Finding Represents

  • Papilledema is optic-disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure. Other disc disorders and pseudopapilledema can look similar and may require experienced ophthalmic review.
    • Measure BP to identify a hypertensive emergency and examine acuity, pupils, fields and the fundus. Document severity with photographs or OCT when available.
    • Central acuity can be normal early. Formal fields can reveal important loss that changes urgency even when the patient reports only headache.

Investigate the Cause While Protecting Vision

  • Arrange urgent brain imaging with venous assessment when raised pressure is suspected. Exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and cerebral venous thrombosis before assigning an idiopathic label.

questions.question: An adult with confirmed papilledema has no mass or hydrocephalus on routine brain MRI. Which additional investigation is important before diagnosing IIH?

MR or CT venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis

Correct answer: MR or CT venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis

A Normal Structural Scan Is Not the Complete Workup

**Venous sinus thrombosis can produce papilledema and raised CSF pressure without a mass lesion.** A routine MRI report may not answer the venous question.

The IIH consensus pathway calls for CT or MR venography in the urgent investigation, generally within 24 hours. Seek neuroradiology advice when flow artifacts or unusual anatomy make interpretation uncertain.

Assess pregnancy-related, thrombotic, inflammatory and other risks according to context, but absence of a recognized risk factor does not itself exclude thrombosis.

**Complete the neurologic, ocular and laboratory assessment** and perform LP when safe to document pressure and normal CSF composition.

Review medicines and systemic conditions associated with secondary pressure elevation. Obesity, pulsatile tinnitus or an empty sella can support suspicion but do not establish idiopathic disease.

questions.question: After appropriate normal imaging and venography, a patient with suspected IIH undergoes LP while anxious, sitting and straining. The recorded pressure is 29 cm CSF. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Apply a fixed correction factor to convert the sitting pressure into a diagnostic lateral-decubitus value
The value confirms IIH independently of the examination and CSF contents
The measurement is not a reliable standard opening pressure; reassess technique and the full diagnostic evidence
The value excludes IIH because it is below 30 cm CSF
questions.explanation:
Opening Pressure Requires Technique and Context

Correct answer: The measurement is not a reliable standard opening pressure; reassess technique and the full diagnostic evidence

Measure Under Appropriate Conditions

**Measure opening pressure in the lateral decubitus position**, with the patient relaxed and legs extended, allowing the manometer level to settle.

Avoid interpreting straining, breath holding or an improperly positioned recording as the standard value. Document technical limitations and relevant sedation or distress.

The 2018 consensus uses an adult cutoff above 25 cm CSF, while diagnostic frameworks often express an elevated threshold at or above 25; borderline values require clinical interpretation rather than false precision.

A Number Does Not Replace the Syndrome

**Pressure must be interpreted with papilledema, neurologic findings, imaging and normal CSF composition.** Exclude secondary causes before assigning an idiopathic label.

A single measurement samples a fluctuating physiologic variable. If it conflicts with a convincing syndrome, expert review may support repeat assessment rather than automatic acceptance or exclusion.

Do not perform repeated LP simply to chase a number or use an unsafe procedure when structural contraindications exist. Assess visual risk throughout the workup. The need for urgent vision-protecting treatment is determined by the clinical state, not by waiting for an arbitrarily more dramatic pressure reading.

Apply a fixed correction factor to convert the sitting pressure into a diagnostic lateral-decubitus value: There is no universal arithmetic correction that replaces an appropriately obtained measurement; position and straining can materially affect interpretation.

The value confirms IIH independently of the examination and CSF contents: An elevated pressure alone does not establish idiopathic disease, especially when technique is nonstandard; visual, imaging, CSF and exclusion findings remain necessary.

The value excludes IIH because it is below 30 cm CSF: Adult diagnostic thresholds are around 25 cm CSF rather than a universal 30-cm cutoff; the issue here is reliability and integrated interpretation.

questions.question: A patient develops papilledema and raised CSF pressure after starting doxycycline. Brain imaging and venography exclude structural and thrombotic causes. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Retain an idiopathic diagnosis because venography is negative
Review and withdraw the suspected medicine through a coordinated plan while protecting vision and assessing other contributors
Continue doxycycline and treat the pressure without reviewing its indication
Use the timing alone as sufficient proof and omit visual follow-up
questions.explanation:
Medicine-Associated Intracranial Hypertension

Correct answer: Review and withdraw the suspected medicine through a coordinated plan while protecting vision and assessing other contributors

Look Beyond the Usual Demographic Pattern

**Tetracyclines and vitamin A derivatives are important medication associations** with intracranial hypertension. Review prescriptions, supplements and recent changes.

Other medicines and systemic conditions have been reported, but the strength of causal evidence varies. Do not describe every historical association as an equally established cause.

Obesity or a typical demographic profile does not make secondary evaluation unnecessary. A medication-associated syndrome can resemble IIH clinically.

Remove Contributors Without Delaying Vision Care

**Discuss cessation or substitution with the treating clinician**, considering the original indication and the seriousness of the neurologic problem.

Document visual acuity, fields and disc status and treat pressure-related visual risk according to severity. Drug withdrawal is not a reason to wait passively when vision is deteriorating.

Continue assessment of other contributors and follow objective improvement. Re-exposure should be considered carefully rather than used as a diagnostic challenge. Explain that a plausible drug association does not guarantee immediate resolution and that persistent symptoms require reassessment for another cause or ongoing pressure injury.

Retain an idiopathic diagnosis because venography is negative: Negative venography excludes one important mechanism, but does not eliminate medicine-associated or other secondary pressure elevation.

Continue doxycycline and treat the pressure without reviewing its indication: Pressure treatment may be necessary, but failure to address a plausible medication trigger can perpetuate the problem when alternatives are available.

Use the timing alone as sufficient proof and omit visual follow-up: The temporal relationship supports suspicion but does not prove exclusive causality or remove the need to monitor and protect visual function.

questions.question: A woman with active IIH and BMI 39 has stable mild visual loss under specialist monitoring. Which long-term intervention addresses a central disease-modifying mechanism?
options: Repeated therapeutic LP as the long-term disease-modifying intervention
A supported sustained weight-loss strategy, including bariatric assessment when appropriate
Analgesic escalation as the principal way to reverse the underlying disease
Permanent high-dose corticosteroids to maintain pressure remission
questions.explanation:
Sustained Weight Loss in Typical IIH

Correct answer: A supported sustained weight-loss strategy, including bariatric assessment when appropriate

Treat Weight as a Supported Medical Intervention

**Sustained weight loss can reduce intracranial pressure in typical obesity-associated IIH.** Discuss structured care without attributing the illness to personal failure.

The IIH Weight Trial enrolled women with active disease and BMI at least 35 and found greater sustained pressure reduction with bariatric surgery than community weight management.

This evidence applies to an eligible selected population, not a mandate for surgery in every patient. Assess comorbidity, nutritional needs, preferences and local eligibility.

Weight Management Does Not Replace Immediate Visual Protection

**Continue pressure-lowering and visual-monitoring treatment as indicated.** Rapidly worsening vision requires urgent intervention rather than waiting for weight loss.

Lifestyle, specialist obesity pharmacotherapy and metabolic surgery have different evidence, risks and access; choose an individualized sustainable plan and monitor its effect.

Follow papilledema and fields as well as weight and headache. Weight regain can be associated with recurrence, so long-term support matters. A patient may have persistent migraine-like headache despite pressure improvement; distinguish that symptom burden from active sight-threatening disease rather than escalating pressure procedures solely because pain continues.

Repeated therapeutic LP as the long-term disease-modifying intervention: LP can temporarily reduce CSF pressure in selected circumstances, but fluid is replenished and serial punctures are not the preferred sustained disease-modifying strategy.

Analgesic escalation as the principal way to reverse the underlying disease: Headache treatment is important, but analgesia does not address the pressure-related disease mechanism and overuse can add another headache problem.

Permanent high-dose corticosteroids to maintain pressure remission: Long-term steroids add substantial toxicity and can promote weight gain; they are not the recommended disease-modifying strategy for typical IIH.

questions.question: A patient with confirmed IIH and mild visual field loss is starting acetazolamide alongside weight management. Which prescribing approach is most appropriate?
options: Keep 250 mg twice daily fixed irrespective of visual course
Start 2 g twice daily and reduce only after visual remission
Use 250 mg intermittently for severe headache days
Start 250–500 mg twice daily and titrate to response and tolerability
questions.explanation:
Acetazolamide for IIH With Mild Visual Loss

Correct answer: Start 250–500 mg twice daily and titrate to response and tolerability

Use Evidence Within Its Clinical Population

**Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase and reduces CSF production.** Trial evidence shows modest visual-field benefit when added to a weight-reduction diet in patients with mild visual loss.

A common starting range is ==250–500 mg twice daily==, increasing as tolerated. The trial maximum was ==4 g/day==, not a required target for all patients.

Severe or rapidly progressive visual decline requires urgent procedural assessment; tablets should not be used to postpone needed vision-protecting intervention.

Anticipate Toxicity and Monitor Function

**Discuss paresthesia, fatigue, altered taste and gastrointestinal effects**, as well as metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbance and renal stone risk.

Review kidney function, bicarbonate/electrolytes and relevant contraindications or interactions. Pregnancy and reproductive counseling require individualized specialist advice.

Follow formal visual fields and disc findings, not just headache intensity. Adjust or change treatment when intolerance prevents a useful course rather than urging an unsustainable dose. Continue weight management and a separate headache strategy where needed; acetazolamide benefit for vision does not establish it as effective treatment of headache alone.

Keep 250 mg twice daily fixed irrespective of visual course: A low starting dose can suit some patients, but titration or a change of strategy must reflect visual response and toxicity rather than an unreviewed fixed prescription.

Start 2 g twice daily and reduce only after visual remission: Four grams daily was a trial maximum, but starting immediately at that dose can be poorly tolerated and is not necessary for every patient.

Use 250 mg intermittently for severe headache days: Acetazolamide is used as sustained pressure-lowering treatment when indicated, not as an as-needed acute headache analgesic.

questions.question: A patient with confirmed IIH has rapidly worsening visual fields and papilledema despite medical therapy. Which next approach is most appropriate?

questions.explanation:
Rapid Visual Deterioration in IIH

Correct answer: Arrange urgent vision-protecting procedural assessment

Treat Vision Loss as the Urgent Endpoint

**Declining visual function in IIH requires urgent intervention planning.** Formal fields, acuity and disc findings define the threat more reliably than headache severity alone.

Confirm the trend and coordinate neuro-ophthalmology and neurosurgery promptly. Do not wait for profound central acuity loss before escalating.

A temporizing CSF drainage strategy may be used by specialists while definitive treatment is arranged, with appropriate procedural safety assessment.

Individualize the Procedure and Follow-Up

**CSF diversion and optic nerve sheath fenestration have selected roles**, influenced by visual pattern, overall symptoms, local expertise and patient factors.

Shunts can obstruct, become infected or cause overdrainage; fenestration also has procedural risks and does not treat every aspect of the pressure syndrome. Venous stenting is not an automatic replacement based on narrowing alone.

Continue disease modification and objective visual monitoring after intervention. A technically successful procedure does not guarantee recovery of established optic atrophy. Recurrent headache or visual change needs reassessment for active pressure, treatment complications and other mechanisms rather than automatic repetition of the original operation.

Increase acetazolamide and review fields at the next routine clinic: Dose adjustment can help stable disease, but rapid field deterioration requires urgent intervention planning and should not await routine reassessment.

questions.question: A patient previously treated for IIH has stable visual fields and resolved papilledema but persistent migraine-like headache with frequent analgesic use. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Escalate acetazolamide until pain stops despite stable ocular findings
Perform regular therapeutic LP solely to maintain headache relief
Recommend CSF diversion solely because headache persists
Assess headache phenotype and medication overuse while maintaining appropriate visual surveillance
questions.explanation:
Persistent Headache After Papilledema Resolves

Correct answer: Assess headache phenotype and medication overuse while maintaining appropriate visual surveillance

Separate Ocular Remission From Symptom Burden

**Headache can persist after the pressure-related ocular disease improves.** Migraine biology, medication overuse and other contributors can coexist with prior IIH.

Review frequency, triggers, positional features and analgesic days. New visual symptoms or an altered pattern warrants renewed assessment rather than assuming every headache is the same.

Continue an appropriate follow-up plan for recurrence risk; resolved papilledema does not mean the patient’s pain is unimportant or that future pressure disease is impossible.

Use a Headache-Specific Plan

**Treat the demonstrated headache phenotype**, including medication-overuse management and suitable preventive therapy when indicated.

Choose medicines with attention to weight, mood, cognition, reproductive considerations and existing treatment. Explain that pain relief and visual protection are separate treatment goals.

Serial LP is not routine long-term care, and CSF diversion should not be recommended solely from persistent pain without expert evaluation. If symptoms suggest shunt malfunction or low pressure in a previously operated patient, investigate those possibilities specifically. Objective visual and neurologic reassessment helps avoid both unnecessary pressure procedures and dismissal of a genuine recurrence.

questions.question: A patient with a posterior-fossa mass develops vomiting and reduced consciousness. CT shows ventricular enlargement proximal to an obstructed CSF pathway. Which next approach is most appropriate?
options: Urgent neurosurgical assessment for controlled ventricular CSF diversion and treatment of the obstruction
Perform a large-volume lumbar puncture as the initial decompression
Treat with acetazolamide and arrange elective imaging review
Begin an outpatient normal-pressure-hydrocephalus tap-test pathway
questions.explanation:
Acute Obstructive Hydrocephalus

Correct answer: Urgent neurosurgical assessment for controlled ventricular CSF diversion and treatment of the obstruction

Identify the Obstruction and Clinical Threat

**Obstructive hydrocephalus results from impaired passage through a CSF pathway.** Imaging defines the level and accompanying mass effect.

Reduced consciousness, vomiting and progressive neurologic signs require emergency assessment and physiologic stabilization. A chronic ventriculomegaly workup must not replace the acute pathway.

Protect airway and perfusion as needed while urgently involving neurosurgery; do not delay action to obtain every elective diagnostic sequence.

Choose Diversion With the Anatomy in Mind

**An external ventricular drain or another appropriate procedure can provide controlled diversion**, with definitive treatment directed at the cause. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy suits selected obstruction patterns, not every hydrocephalus.

Drainage rate and pressure require specialist control because abrupt pressure shifts can be hazardous, particularly with posterior-fossa lesions.

Lumbar puncture is not a safe universal decompression method. Assess infection, hemorrhage and procedural risks and continue monitoring after diversion. Persistent or recurrent deterioration requires review of drain function and the underlying lesion rather than assuming ventricular enlargement alone explains every subsequent problem.

Perform a large-volume lumbar puncture as the initial decompression: A posterior-fossa mass with obstructive pressure gradients can make lumbar drainage dangerous; ventricular and definitive structural treatment require neurosurgical planning.

Treat with acetazolamide and arrange elective imaging review: Medical CSF reduction can have selected roles, but does not adequately address acute neurologic deterioration from an obstructed pathway.

Begin an outpatient normal-pressure-hydrocephalus tap-test pathway: That evaluation concerns a chronic clinical syndrome after appropriate assessment; it is inappropriate for acute obstructive deterioration with a mass lesion.

questions.question: An older adult has gait-predominant impairment, urinary urgency and cognitive slowing. MRI shows ventriculomegaly with a DESH pattern. One tap test shows no clear immediate improvement. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Repeat the LP solely to document a higher opening pressure
Treat the negative immediate test as sufficient to stop the shunt workup
Proceed directly to shunting without assessing competing gait disorders
Reassess test quality, timing, comorbidity and the overall syndrome; a negative tap test does not exclude shunt responsiveness
questions.explanation:
A Negative Tap Test Does Not End an iNPH Evaluation

Correct answer: Reassess test quality, timing, comorbidity and the overall syndrome; a negative tap test does not exclude shunt responsiveness

Recognize the Clinical-Imaging Pattern

**iNPH commonly produces gait impairment with cognitive and urinary symptoms**, but the complete triad is neither uniquely diagnostic nor present in every patient.

DESH includes ventriculomegaly with tight high-convexity spaces and relatively enlarged Sylvian fissures. It supports the diagnosis without making other causes irrelevant.

Assess parkinsonism, neuropathy, vascular disease, orthopedic limitations and neurodegeneration because each can alter gait or expected recovery.

Interpret Drainage Testing as a Predictor With Limits

**Use objective baseline and post-drainage measures**, including gait timing and suitable delayed reassessment. A limited immediate examination can miss a clinically relevant response.

Specialists may consider repeat or extended assessment when the overall suspicion remains high. Neither a negative test nor a DESH pattern alone resolves every treatment decision.

Discuss shunt risks, comorbidity and realistic domain-specific benefit; gait may improve differently from cognition. Do not promise complete reversal of dementia or treat age alone as a veto. Follow function and complications after any procedure and reassess deterioration for malfunction, overdrainage or a coexisting progressive disorder.

Repeat the LP solely to document a higher opening pressure: iNPH assessment is not a search for a high pressure threshold; objective response, clinical pattern and imaging are the relevant questions.

Treat the negative immediate test as sufficient to stop the shunt workup: A negative test can lower confidence, but false negatives and delayed responses occur; the gait phenotype, DESH pattern and assessment quality warrant integrated review.

Proceed directly to shunting without assessing competing gait disorders: The pattern can support a shunt decision in selected patients, but comorbidity and procedural risk still require assessment rather than relying on ventriculomegaly alone.

questions.question: A patient has a new headache that worsens upright and improves recumbent, with supportive brain MRI findings. A previous LP opening pressure was within range. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Low-lying cerebellar tonsils establish congenital Chiari disease as the cause
The pressure excludes SIH and establishes migraine
Repeat LP is required solely to demonstrate low pressure before further imaging
A normal opening pressure does not exclude a spinal CSF leak syndrome
questions.explanation:
Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension With Normal Opening Pressure

Correct answer: A normal opening pressure does not exclude a spinal CSF leak syndrome

A CSF-Volume Disorder Can Have a Normal Measured Pressure

**SIH usually results from a spinal dural leak or CSF-venous fistula.** The syndrome name does not mean that every patient has a low LP reading.

Orthostatic headache is characteristic, but its timing and prominence can evolve. Associated neck, auditory, vestibular or cognitive symptoms can contribute to recognition.

Brain MRI may show pachymeningeal enhancement, venous engorgement, brain sag or subdural collections; normal MRI does not exclude every case.

Investigate Without Creating an Unnecessary Puncture

**First-line imaging generally includes contrast brain MRI and whole-spine MRI.** Spinal imaging can guide the leak pathway but may not localize the exact defect.

Do not perform LP solely to prove low pressure. If CSF sampling is needed for another diagnostic question, discuss its risks and interpret pressure in context.

Assess orthostatic hypotension, postural tachycardia, migraine and other mimics according to symptoms. A strongly suggestive case with normal initial studies warrants expert review rather than automatic dismissal. Significant subdural collections or neurologic decline require urgent specialist assessment, and treating the underlying leak can be central to preventing recurrent complications.

Syndrome | Key clinical clue | Pressure/test interpretation | Safety or management distinction

IIH | Papilledema with appropriate pressure syndrome | Elevated properly measured pressure plus normal CSF and exclusions | Assess venous causes and protect vision

Acute obstruction | Deterioration with obstructed ventricular pathway | Structural imaging defines dangerous gradients | Urgent specialist diversion; LP can be unsafe

iNPH | Gait-predominant chronic syndrome and compatible ventriculomegaly | Tap response can help; a negative test is not absolute exclusion | Assess comorbidity and realistic shunt benefit

SIH | Orthostatic headache with compatible imaging or leak evidence | Normal LP pressure does not exclude disease | Avoid LP solely for confirmation; consider early EBP

The pressure excludes SIH and establishes migraine: Migraine can have positional aggravation, but a normal pressure does not exclude SIH; the orthostatic history and imaging require integrated evaluation.

Repeat LP is required solely to demonstrate low pressure before further imaging: LP is not recommended merely to confirm SIH because pressure can be normal and the procedure can create another leak; appropriate MRI and specialist review come first.

Blood Patch and Leak Localization

Correct answer: Offer an early non-targeted epidural blood patch, with specialist localization if response is absent or transient

options: Test an unaffected relative first because this avoids ambiguity from advanced disease

Define phenotype and pedigree, assess acquired mimics and counsel about scope, limitations and possible results

questions.explanation:
Choose a Genetic Test From the Clinical Question

Correct answer: Define phenotype and pedigree, assess acquired mimics and counsel about scope, limitations and possible results

Make the Diagnostic Question Explicit

**Phenotype and pedigree determine the most informative assay.** Document onset, progression, neurologic domains and relevant systemic features and consider actionable acquired mimics.

A three-generation family history can suggest inheritance but may be limited by small families, variable expression, reduced penetrance or de novo disease.

Testing may require a targeted variant, repeat assay, copy-number method, panel, exome, genome or mitochondrial strategy rather than one universal platform.

Consent Includes Uncertainty and Family Implications

**Discuss pathogenic, negative and uncertain results**, possible secondary findings where relevant, and the practical implications for relatives and reproductive decisions.

Clarify whether testing is diagnostic in an affected person or predictive in someone without symptoms. The counseling and consent requirements differ.

Use an appropriate clinical laboratory and specialist interpretation and explain the possibility of later reanalysis. A result should inform care through established evidence rather than create a diagnosis from a rare sequence change alone. Protect autonomy and confidentiality, and plan how results will be communicated and followed up instead of treating ordering the test as the end of the evaluation.

questions.question: A panel identifies a variant of uncertain significance in a gene associated with the patient’s broad neurologic phenotype. Which next action is most appropriate?
options: Close the molecular evaluation because the gene on the report fits broadly
Use the VUS to select disease-specific surveillance independent of the phenotype
Offer predictive testing to relatives using the VUS as the familial risk marker
Continue clinical evaluation and seek appropriate segregation or reclassification evidence without treating the VUS as causal
questions.explanation:
A VUS Is Not a Confirmed Molecular Diagnosis

Correct answer: Continue clinical evaluation and seek appropriate segregation or reclassification evidence without treating the VUS as causal

Understand the Classification

**A VUS has insufficient evidence for a pathogenic or benign conclusion.** It is not a partial confirmation of disease and should not be used as the basis of clinical decision-making.

Population frequency, segregation, functional evidence, mechanism and phenotype can contribute to later classification. A plausible gene name alone does not establish causality.

A negative or uncertain panel also does not exclude every inherited mechanism; review whether the relevant variant classes were assessed.

Use Family Information for the Right Purpose

**Selected family testing can help resolve uncertainty**, especially when coordinated with the laboratory and genetics service. This is different from treating the VUS as an established predictive marker.

Continue symptom-based care and surveillance justified by the clinical findings or family history, rather than by the uncertain sequence result alone.

Document the interpretation, explain that classification can change and arrange an appropriate recontact or reanalysis process. Avoid providing false reassurance from a benign-sounding uncertain report or imposing major lifestyle and reproductive conclusions from an unsupported causal claim. A later pathogenic reclassification requires renewed phenotype and inheritance review before changing family-specific advice.

Close the molecular evaluation because the gene on the report fits broadly: A plausible gene is not sufficient; evidence may be needed for reclassification, and other mechanisms or diagnoses can still require assessment.

Use the VUS to select disease-specific surveillance independent of the phenotype: Surveillance may be justified by clinical or family findings, but an uncertain variant alone should not be treated as the established causal basis for management.

Offer predictive testing to relatives using the VUS as the familial risk marker: Family testing can help segregation and reclassification, but is not equivalent to predictive testing of an established pathogenic familial variant.
